criterion_notes.c1: While the study is situated in the urban sanitation / fecal sludge management (FSM) sector in Kushtia Municipality (covering household onsite containment, municipal vacutug emptying and transport, and private treatment/co-composting), it examines the financial viability and business-model sustainability of FSM operations across the sanitation value chain rather than household or community sanitation service access. Household toilet typology (Table 5) is cited only as secondary background from an external report (Chowdhury, 2018), and household emptying volumes are treated as fixed inputs into the financial simulator.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper WOULD pass (plain=yes) because it examines institutional, regulatory, and financial governance arrangements for FSM business models—including municipal versus private service operation, compatibility with regulations permitting sanitation taxes up to 12% of holding tax, lease/discharge licenses, and municipal institutional capacity. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, however, it fails (narrow=no): although tariff/cost-recovery instruments (emptying fees, sanitation taxes, discharge fees/licenses) and public/private operator structures are modeled, they are evaluated only as hypothetical revenue-transfer scenarios governing operator financial profitability across the sanitation value chain, not as rules empirically governing household service access. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the full-text decision remains exclude because the paper fails Criteria 1 and 4 (no household service access or affordability outcome).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data collected via 7 key informant interviews, 6 focus group discussions, and 2 joint stakeholder meetings (30 participants), combined with municipal/operator financial records, SWOT analysis, financial flow simulation (eSOSView™) of existing and hypothetical models, and stakeholder multi-criteria analysis (FIETS).
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report an empirical outcome of household sanitation access, connection, service availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. The reported outcomes are operator and value-chain financial viability metrics (CAPEX, OPEX, revenue, and annual net profit/loss in USD/year in Table 7) and stakeholder FIETS multi-criteria scores (Table 8) used to select a business model. The FIETS 'public acceptance and affordability' sub-score (assigning 7 instead of 10 to hypothetical models 3-6 solely because they add a hypothetical sanitation tax) is an ex-ante subjective decision-analysis weight for unimplemented models, not an empirical measurement of household affordability or service access.
criterion_notes.c5: The study design (mixed-methods case study with eSOSView™ financial simulation and FIETS multi-criteria analysis), setting/sample in Kushtia Municipality, unit of analysis (7 financial flow models across the sanitation value chain), compared model configurations, and financial/MCDA outcomes are clearly identifiable, allowing definitive exclusion on outcome/scope grounds.

evidence_quotes.quote: Hence, this study was conducted in Kushtia Municipality with three main objectives: 1) to investigate current FSM practices to analyze existing FSM, 2) to study ﬁnancial transfers to analyze the ﬁnancial viability of existing FFMs, and 3) to evaluate various FFMs/business models to recommend a sustainable model.
Primary data, both quantitative and qualitative were collected from key informant interviews and focus group discussions (Table 3).
For E&T, the existing models, models 2 and 6 scored 2.5 because of supportive regulations for the privatization of services and imposing sanitation tax up to 12% of holding tax.

The ﬁnancial analysis of existing FFMs in Kushtia revealed that it is ﬁnancially unviable, incurring a loss of 3,901 USD per year. While exploring other FFMs, it showed that the modiﬁed parallel tax and discharge fee model generates the highest net proﬁt of 51,396 USD per year considering the entire SVC (49,863 USD per year for E&T and 1,533 USD per year for treatment and reuse).

For E&T, the existing model and models 1 and 2 scored 10, as these do not include any additional charge to public, whereas models 3, 4, 5, and 6 scored 7 as they add sanitation tax which is an additional expenditure for households.

raw_response.exposure: Simulated fecal sludge management financial flow and business models varying emptying fees, hypothetical sanitation taxes, discharge fees/licenses/incentives, lease fees, and public versus private operation of emptying/transport and treatment/reuse
raw_response.outcome: Service-provider and sanitation-value-chain financial viability (annual CAPEX, OPEX, revenue, and net profit/loss in USD/year) and stakeholder FIETS multi-criteria sustainability scores (0-100) for business model selection
raw_response.population_and_sample: Kushtia Municipality sanitation value chain (city population 418,312 in 93,582 households / 33,250 holdings; municipal vacutug emptying and transport service and private fecal sludge treatment/co-compost plant); primary data from 7 key informant interviews, 6 focus group discussions with residents, and 2 joint stakeholder meetings (30 participants); unit of analysis is 7 financial flow models (existing model plus 6 simulated models)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome). This study applies the eSOSView™ financial flow simulator and a stakeholder FIETS multi-criteria analysis in Kushtia Municipality, Bangladesh, to assess the financial viability of existing fecal sludge management (FSM) operations and compare six hypothetical financial flow/business models (varying emptying fees, assumed sanitation taxes, discharge fees/licenses, and public vs. private operation). Its measured outcomes are operator and sanitation-value-chain financial performance (CAPEX, OPEX, revenue, and annual net profit/loss in USD/year) and ex-ante stakeholder multi-criteria scores for business-model sustainability, rather than empirical household sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, affordability, or exclusion outcomes. Under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study is excluded for lacking a household service-access outcome.
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods case study combining financial flow simulation (eSOSView™) and stakeholder multi-criteria decision analysis (FIETS), informed by key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and joint stakeholder meetings
